1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Marrowgate Components (fictional) is a contract molder. At its Tollbridge plant, Line B molds the VX family of connector housings (VX-12, VX-18, VX-24) from glass-filled nylon (PA66-GF30) on injection Presses 5 and 7. All other Line B product families are polypropylene. Each press has its own desiccant resin dryer: D5 feeds Press 5 and D7 feeds Press 7. Until week 36, all VX resin came from Quillan Polymers. In week 37 a second supplier, Arnholt Resins, was released for general use. VX rejects at final snap-fit and visual inspection have risen every week since then.
9	Your request: The operations director writes: 'VX rejects are close to 4% and climbing, and a customer has opened an 8D. I have three people giving me three different stories. Tell me what is actually driving this and what we should do this week. The ops manager wants to act on the new second-shift operators, the plant manager's instinct is to drop Arnholt, and maintenance say the dryers are fine.'
10	Initial evidence:
11	- Line B quality dashboard export, generated Monday of week 43 (system-record): VX family (VX-12/18/24), % of parts rejected at final snap-fit and visual inspection, all presses combined: wks 30–36: 0.7–0.8% each week; wk 37 1.3; wk 38 1.9; wk 39 2.5; wk 40 3.0; wk 41 3.4; wk 42 3.7. Rejects by shift, wks 37–42: first shift 2.1% of 72,000 parts; second shift 3.7% of 36,000 parts. Reject codes, wks 37–42: latch crack at snap-fit 61%, splay/silver streaks 32%, short shot 7%. Polypropylene families on Line B: flat at 0.4–0.6% throughout. No engineering change to VX drawings, materials specification or test limits since March.
12	- Email from R. Valdez-Hunt, Operations Manager, to the Operations Director, week 43 (manager-account): Subject: VX rejects – my read. Second shift is running nearly double first shift's reject rate. It started the week after we brought on six new operators (wk 36). Nothing else lines up. Arnholt resin came through a three-week trial with no issues, and maintenance confirm the dryers are not the problem: Press 5 ran clean all summer. I propose putting the six on performance improvement plans and taking them off VX until they are re-certified. The plant manager's first instinct was to drop Arnholt, but the trial data doesn't support that and procurement would fight it. I'd rather fix the people side now than wait for another study.
13	- Supplier Quality memo SQ-0912, T. Brennan (Supplier Quality Engineer), week 36 (document): Arnholt Resins PA66-GF30 production trial, wks 34–36, run on Press 7 only (Press 7 is Line B's designated trial press). Result: 7,800 VX parts, 0.7% rejects against the 0.8% Quillan baseline. Dimensional and snap-fit results are equivalent. The certificates of analysis for all three trial lots state moisture 'conforms, spec ≤0.35%'. Recommendation: approve Arnholt as second source and release it to general use from wk 37 on both VX presses, issued FIFO by stores. Logistics note: Arnholt ships in 1-tonne octabins that do not fit the main-warehouse racks, so stores will hold them in the north annex.
14	- Interview notes, Line B maintenance technician, week 43 (staff-account): 'D5 has been running wet dew points since late July: −15 to −20 instead of −40. The regeneration heater trips now and then, and the desiccant is due. It alarmed constantly and kept stopping the press, so in wk 31 we put it through the change board and moved the alarm limit to −15. But look: Press 5 ran Quillan the whole of August into mid-September at normal rejects with D5 exactly like that. If the dryer were the problem it would have shown up then. D7 is fine; it reads −42.' Interviewer note: the heater work order is open and no desiccant change is scheduled.
15	- HR onboarding summary, Line B, week 37 (system-record): Six new molding operators started on Line B second shift on the Monday of wk 36. Before that they completed a two-week classroom and shadowing programme. All six were signed off on the VX and polypropylene work instructions by the end of wk 37. Line B second-shift headcount rose from 9 to 15. First-shift staffing did not change between wks 30 and 42, and neither did supervision on either shift. Exit interviews and absence for the period show nothing unusual.
16	
17	BRIEF:
18	The rejects come from an interaction between two things. Arnholt resin arrives wetter than Quillan (0.27–0.33% against 0.11–0.14%). Dryer D5 has degraded, with a dew point of about −16 °C instead of −40 °C. D5 can't dry Arnholt below the 0.20% limit, so Press 5 makes cracked and splayed parts. Rates by press and resin:
19	- Press 5 on Arnholt: 9.9% rejects.
20	- Press 5 on Quillan: 0.9%.
21	- Press 7 on Arnholt: 0.8%.
22	- Press 7 on Quillan: 0.7%.
23	The same Arnholt lot gave 10.4% rejects through D5 and 0.8% through a good dryer.
24	
25	Second shift only looks worse because all its VX work runs on Press 5. Within that shift, new and experienced operators have the same rates. Don't discipline the new operators, and don't drop Arnholt.
26	
27	Do this week:
28	1. Repair D5, meaning the heater and desiccant.
29	2. Restore the alarm limit that was loosened to −15.
30	3. Keep Arnholt off D5 until D5 is verified.
31	4. Check moisture at the press feed throat for every resin lot.
32	
33	Answer the 8D with this cause. I'm quite confident in this cause. One thing is unresolved: whether the north annex storage is why Arnholt arrives wetter. Every Arnholt sample came from the annex, so supplier and storage can't be separated. Moving the octabins is premature. Check Arnholt moisture in sealed packaging first.
34
